metadata.title: Student Characteristics and ICT Usage as Predictors of Computational Thinking: An Explainable AI Approach

survey_design.weight_fields_interpretation: The study uses ICILS 2023 Grade 8 student microdata and restricts the analytic sample to students with complete CT assessment data (81,871 students across 23 countries plus one regional education system). The manuscript does not report whether ICILS complex survey sampling weights (and any replicate weights) were applied in the LightGBM/Random Forest training and SHAP interpretation, so weight usage cannot be confirmed from the provided text. Because the models are tree-based ML methods, the authors may have proceeded with unweighted estimation; however, the paper does not explicitly state this. For replication with ICILS Data, analysts should use the ICILS-provided student sampling weights (and replicate weights if variance estimation is required) and ensure that any preprocessing steps (feature filtering, normalization, SMOTE, and feature selection) are performed within resampling folds to avoid leakage.

sample_details.sample_filtering_criteria: Data were drawn from ICILS 2023 and restricted to the subsample with complete CT assessment data. The CT outcome was computed from five plausible values (abstraction, algorithmic thinking, automation, decomposition, debugging) and then averaged to form a composite CT score. For preprocessing, variables with more than 40% missing values were removed, and features with zero variance were eliminated. The final modeling dataset used a hierarchical feature engineering pipeline that retained the top 30 predictive features (LightGBM feature importance; p < 0.05) and then reduced to a final set of 10 core features using LightGBM plus GridSearchCV.

confounders_identified.variable_name: Academic ICT use outside school (non-school days)

main_findings.target_variable: Computational thinking composite score (average of five PVs)
main_findings.performance_metrics: LightGBM feature selection + Random Forest classifier; ROC/AUC reported during feature subset optimization with maximum AUC = 0.72 on the test set; 10-fold cross-validation used for stability. Exact final-model AUC for the 10-feature model not reported in the provided text.
main_findings.standardized_conclusion: Using ICILS 2023 Grade 8 Computational Thinking the study leveraged educational expectations, books at home, and multiple ICT-usage context variables to predict computational thinking (composite score averaged across five plausible values), finding that several predictors show nonlinear relationships (including U-shaped and inverted U-shaped patterns) and that SHAP-enabled interpretation reveals context-dependent ICT effects. This indicates that ICT-integrated instructional design should be tailored by course context and student goal orientation rather than assuming that more ICT use uniformly improves computational thinking, while causality cannot be inferred from cross-sectional predictive SHAP patterns.

data.outcome_summary: The study uses ICILS 2023 Grade 8 data, restricting to 81,871 students from 23 countries plus one regional education system (North Rhine-Westphalia, Germany) who completed the CT assessment. Computational thinking is measured via four CT modules and summarized as a composite score averaged across five plausible values (abstraction, algorithmic thinking, automation, decomposition, debugging). The authors build an explainable predictive framework combining LightGBM for feature ranking/selection and a Random Forest classifier for the final explanatory analysis, using SHAP (TreeExplainer) to characterize nonlinear effects. During feature subset optimization, the ROC analysis reports a maximum test-set AUC of 0.72, and the selected top 10 features show stable contributions across 10-fold cross-validation. Limitations include the absence of explicit reporting on survey-weight use and the fact that SHAP-based importance and dependence plots support prediction and interpretation, not causal claims.
